title: Pillar V — Tailwind, Layouts & Stacking Contexts

sections.heading: Utility-first: what Tailwind actually is
paragraphs: Tailwind is a set of tiny single-purpose classes — `flex`, `p-4`, `text-slate-200` — composed directly in markup instead of writing named CSS classes in a stylesheet. Styles live next to the structure they style, and there's no naming ceremony or dead-CSS archaeology.

It's still just CSS: `p-4` is `padding: 1rem` on a spacing scale, colors come from a palette, breakpoints from a scale. The constraint is the point — a design system's worth of consistent values, enforced by what classes exist.

At build time, Tailwind scans your source for class names and generates only the CSS you actually used. Which is why dynamically assembled class strings like `text-${color}-500` silently fail: the scanner never sees the complete name, so it never generates the rule.
sections.summary: Tailwind is just tiny CSS shortcuts you write right in your markup, and it only builds classes it can spot written out in full.

variants.question: A developer writes `className={`bg-${theme}-500`}` and the background silently never appears in production. Why?
options: Tailwind's build-time scan looks for complete class names in source; a name assembled at runtime is never seen, so its CSS is never generated
The bg- prefix requires a corresponding text- class to activate
Colors in Tailwind only work with inline styles
Template literals aren't allowed in the className attribute
variants.rationale: Tailwind doesn't execute your code — it greps it. `bg-${theme}-500` contains no complete class name to find. The fix is a map of full names: `{ red: 'bg-red-500', blue: 'bg-blue-500' }[theme]` — every candidate class appears verbatim somewhere in source.
optionExplanations: Correct — static extraction is the mental model that explains this and several other Tailwind surprises.
Utilities are independent; no class requires a partner class.
Tailwind is classes, not inline styles — colors work everywhere the full class name is written out.
Template literals are fine in JSX — the runtime string is legal; it's the build-time scan that never saw it.
variants.interviewTip: 'Why is my dynamic Tailwind class not working?' is a real-world debugging question that doubles as an interview question. 'Tailwind scans source text, it doesn't run code' is the crisp answer.

variants.question: A team ships a heatmap where each cell's shade comes from `className={`w-4 h-4 bg-${intensity}`}` with `intensity` resolving to strings like `red-300` or `red-700`. In dev everything renders; in the production build every cell is transparent. What single change reliably fixes this?
options: Add `!important` to each cell's background so the production purge can't strip it
Move the color to an inline `style` attribute or select from a map where each full class name (`bg-red-300`, `bg-red-700`, …) appears literally in source
Import the full Tailwind stylesheet unminified so no classes are dropped
Wrap the JSX in a client component so the class is evaluated in the browser instead of at build time
variants.rationale: The dev/prod split is the tell: dev often has a broader/JIT-generated safelist while the production build only emits classes it statically found in source. `bg-${intensity}` is never a complete token, so `bg-red-700` et al. are never generated. Writing every full class name verbatim (via a lookup map), or computing the color as an inline style, both give the build something real to see.
optionExplanations: `!important` changes cascade priority, not whether the rule exists; the CSS was never generated, so there's nothing for `!important` to strengthen.
Correct — the build only generates class names it finds literally in source; a full-name map or an inline style value both satisfy that requirement.
There is no 'full stylesheet' — Tailwind generates on demand; shipping an unpurged build isn't an option in modern Tailwind and wouldn't include a name that was never written out.
Client vs. server rendering is irrelevant — extraction happens at build time regardless of where the component runs; the browser never gets a rule that was never emitted.
variants.interviewTip: When a bug reproduces only in the production build and not in dev, suspect build-time class extraction (or tree-shaking/purging) before suspecting runtime logic — that 'works in dev, breaks in prod' signature is the giveaway.

variants.question: A dashboard lets admins pick an accent color stored in the database, rendered as `` `border-${accent}-400` ``. The team knows every possible value up front (`sky`, `rose`, `amber`). Which approach makes Tailwind reliably generate the needed CSS?
options: Enable the JIT compiler in the config — it evaluates JavaScript expressions and can resolve the template literal at build time
Declare the color names (`sky`, `rose`, `amber`) in a config array so Tailwind can combine them with utility prefixes during generation
Write every complete class (`border-sky-400`, `border-rose-400`, `border-amber-400`) verbatim — either in a lookup map keyed by the stored value, or in the config's `safelist`
Switch to `border-[${accent}]-400` — the arbitrary-value brackets signal the scanner to accept runtime substitution
variants.rationale: Because the set of values is finite and known, the fix is to make every full class name exist somewhere the scanner can see it: a `{ sky: 'border-sky-400', ... }` map in source, or the `safelist` config option, which force-generates listed classes regardless of whether they're found in source. Both satisfy the same underlying rule — the build needs whole tokens, not fragments.
optionExplanations: JIT changed *when* CSS is generated, not *how* classes are discovered — it still performs a text scan of source files and never executes your code.
No such combination step exists — Tailwind extracts complete class-shaped tokens from text; it never assembles prefixes and values from separate config lists.
Correct — a full-name lookup map or a `safelist` entry gives the scanner (or the generator) complete tokens, which is the only thing it can work with.
Arbitrary-value brackets still have to appear as a complete literal token in source; interpolating inside them is exactly as invisible to the scanner as any other template fragment.
variants.interviewTip: Mentioning `safelist` alongside the lookup-map fix shows depth: the map is the everyday answer, but safelist is the escape hatch for genuinely data-driven classes — knowing when each applies is a senior-level distinction.

variants.question: Conceptually, why can Tailwind's build step generate CSS for `md:hover:bg-indigo-600` written literally in a file, but not for the identical string produced at runtime by `` `md:hover:bg-${shade}-600` ``?
options: Modifier prefixes like `md:` and `hover:` can only be resolved statically, so any class using them must be a literal
Tailwind's scanner runs in the browser, and template literals are only evaluated on the server
Bundlers hoist literal strings into the CSS pipeline but leave template literals in the JavaScript bundle
The build step is a text scan over raw source files, not a JavaScript evaluator — it extracts complete class-shaped tokens from text, so a token that only exists after evaluation is invisible to it
variants.rationale: Tailwind's extractor is deliberately dumb: it treats every source file as plain text and pulls out anything shaped like a class name. It has no idea what `${shade}` will become because it never runs your program. The literal string contains the whole token; the template produces it only at runtime, long after CSS generation finished.
optionExplanations: Modifiers are irrelevant to the distinction — an unmodified `bg-${shade}-600` fails identically, and a literal `md:hover:bg-indigo-600` works fine.
The scanner runs at build time on the developer's machine or CI, never in the browser — and where the literal evaluates has nothing to do with extraction.
Bundler hoisting is fiction here — Tailwind's extraction is independent of the JS bundler's treatment of strings.
Correct — 'text scan, not code execution' is the single mechanism behind every dynamic-class failure mode.
variants.interviewTip: If you can state the mechanism ('Tailwind greps source text; it never evaluates code'), you can derive every rule about dynamic classes on the spot instead of memorizing them — interviewers notice the difference between derivation and recall.

sections.heading: Flexbox: one-dimensional layout
paragraphs: Flexbox lays out children along one axis. The container declares `flex`; direction picks the main axis (`flex-row`, `flex-col`); `justify-*` distributes along the main axis; `items-*` aligns on the cross axis; `gap-*` spaces children.
The mental model that prevents confusion: justify = main axis, items = cross axis, and both rotate when direction changes. In `flex-col`, `justify-center` centers *vertically*.

Children flex too: `flex-1` lets an element grow and shrink to fill remaining space. The everyday patterns: `flex items-center justify-between` for a navbar; a `flex-col` with a `flex-1` middle region for full-height app shells — exactly how this app's own layout works.
sections.summary: Flexbox arranges things in a line: `justify` spaces them along that line and `items` lines them up across it, and both flip when the direction does.

variants.question: Inside a `flex flex-col h-screen` container, which class centers children horizontally?
options: self-center on the container
justify-center
items-center
content-center
variants.rationale: With flex-col, the main axis is vertical — so justify-* controls vertical distribution and items-* controls the horizontal (cross) axis. items-center centers children horizontally here. The axes rotating with direction is the whole trick.
optionExplanations: self-* applies to a flex *child* overriding its own alignment — meaningless on the container.
In a column, justify-center centers *vertically* — the exact inverse of what's asked. This is the most common flexbox mix-up in existence.
Correct — cross axis in a column is horizontal; items-center wins.
content-center affects multi-line/wrapped content lines, not individual child alignment in a single-line flex container.
variants.interviewTip: Live-coding layout under observation is common. Narrate the axis out loud — 'column, so main axis is vertical, so I need items-center for horizontal' — it prevents the error and shows systematic thinking.

variants.question: You have `flex flex-row` toolbar and you want its icon buttons pushed hard against the right edge while staying vertically centered within the bar's height. Which pair of utilities does exactly that?
options: `justify-center self-end`
`content-end items-center`
`items-end justify-center`
`justify-end items-center`
variants.rationale: In `flex-row` the main axis is horizontal, so `justify-end` pushes children to the right edge; the cross axis is vertical, so `items-center` vertically centers them within the bar. The two concerns map to different properties precisely because the axes differ.
optionExplanations: `justify-center` horizontally centers rather than right-aligning, and `self-end` is a child-level override that does nothing meaningful on the container.
`content-end` only affects spacing between *wrapped* flex lines, not single-line horizontal placement, so it won't right-align the buttons.
`items-end` aligns children to the *bottom* (cross axis in a row), not centered vertically, and `justify-center` centers them horizontally instead of pushing them right — both halves wrong.
Correct — main-axis `justify-end` sends them right, cross-axis `items-center` centers them vertically.
variants.interviewTip: Reframe every alignment ask as 'which axis?' first. Once you name the main axis for the current direction, `justify` vs. `items` picks itself — and you avoid the row/column inversion that trips most people up under pressure.

variants.question: A `flex flex-col h-full` sidebar has a single logout block as its only child, and the design pins that block to the sidebar's bottom edge while it stays stretched to the sidebar's full width. Which container class does the pinning?
options: `justify-end` — in a column the main axis runs vertically, so main-axis distribution controls top-to-bottom placement
`items-end` — end alignment always refers to the bottom edge of the container
`content-end` — it shifts the container's content block downward
`align-bottom` — the vertical-align utility anchors flex children to the bottom
variants.rationale: With `flex-col`, vertical placement is a *main-axis* question, so `justify-end` pushes the lone child to the bottom. Crucially, cross-axis stretch (the default `items-stretch`) is untouched, so the block keeps its full width — using `items-end` instead would both fail to move it down and collapse its width.
optionExplanations: Correct — column direction makes vertical distribution the job of `justify-*`, and leaving `items-*` alone preserves the full-width stretch.
In a column, `items-end` acts on the *horizontal* cross axis: it shoves the child to the right and, worse, cancels the default stretch that gave it full width.
`content-*` utilities only matter when wrapped flex lines exist; with a single child in a non-wrapping container they do nothing.
`align-bottom` maps to CSS `vertical-align`, which applies to inline and table-cell contexts — it has zero effect on flex children.
variants.interviewTip: The bottom-pinned sidebar footer is a live-coding staple. Bonus points for mentioning the alternative idiom — `mt-auto` on the child — and explaining that auto margins absorb free main-axis space, which works even with multiple children above.

variants.question: A message row is styled `flex justify-between items-center`. For a mobile redesign the developer changes it to `flex flex-col md:flex-row justify-between items-center`. On phones (below 768px), what do `justify-between` and `items-center` now control?
options: They keep their original row meanings — alignment utilities lock onto the axes of the first direction the container had
`justify-between` now distributes the children vertically and `items-center` centers them horizontally — the properties track the main and cross axes, and those axes rotate with `flex-col`
Both are ignored below `md`, because alignment utilities need a matching direction prefix like `max-md:justify-between` to apply in the column layout
`justify-between` still spaces the children horizontally, but `items-center` flips to vertical centering — only cross-axis utilities rotate with direction
variants.rationale: `justify-*` and `items-*` are bound to the main and cross axes, not to fixed screen directions. When `flex-col` takes effect on phones, the main axis becomes vertical: `justify-between` spreads children top-to-bottom and `items-center` centers each one horizontally. At `md` and up the row returns and both revert to their familiar meanings — same classes, rotated axes.
optionExplanations: There is no locking — alignment resolves against whatever the direction is at the current breakpoint, which is exactly why responsive direction changes silently change what alignment utilities do.
Correct — axis-relative semantics mean one class string produces two different visual behaviors across the breakpoint, which is either a feature or a bug depending on whether you planned for it.
Unprefixed utilities apply at every width; nothing about changing direction requires re-declaring alignment with breakpoint prefixes.
Both properties rotate together — main and cross axes swap as a pair; there's no rule that exempts `justify-*`.
variants.interviewTip: Whenever you add a responsive `flex-col`/`flex-row` switch, immediately re-audit every `justify-*` and `items-*` on that container — their visual meaning just changed at one breakpoint. Saying this unprompted in a review scenario reads as hard-won experience.

sections.heading: Grid and responsive design
paragraphs: Grid is two-dimensional: `grid grid-cols-3 gap-4` gives three columns with row and column tracks managed together. Reach for grid when both dimensions matter (galleries, dashboards) and flexbox when content flows along one line.

Tailwind is mobile-first: unprefixed utilities apply everywhere; prefixed ones override upward. `grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4` means one column by default, two from 768px, four from 1024px.
The common inversion bug: thinking `md:` means 'on medium screens and below'. It means 'at the md breakpoint and up'. Write the phone layout with bare utilities, then layer wider layouts on top.
sections.summary: Grid handles rows and columns together, and prefixes like `md:` mean "this size and bigger," so style phones first and add wider layouts on top.

variants.question: What does `class="grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-3"` produce on a phone (viewport below 768px)?
options: One column — bare utilities are the mobile baseline; md:grid-cols-3 only kicks in at 768px and up
An error, because two grid-cols utilities conflict
Three columns squeezed to fit the narrow screen
Three columns — md: styles apply to medium screens and smaller
variants.rationale: Mobile-first means unprefixed classes are the default at every width, and each breakpoint prefix adds a min-width override. Below 768px only grid-cols-1 applies; at 768px+ the md: rule takes over.
optionExplanations: Correct — baseline unprefixed, overrides layered upward.
Both classes coexist by design; media queries decide which wins at each width. That's the whole responsive system.
Nothing squeezes — the three-column rule simply isn't active below its breakpoint.
This is the classic inversion — md: is min-width (and up), not max-width (and down).
variants.interviewTip: Say 'mobile-first, so breakpoint prefixes are min-width overrides' in any responsive-design discussion — one sentence that demonstrates you understand the cascade, not just the syntax.

variants.question: A designer wants a gallery that is 2 columns on tablets and 4 columns on large desktops, but a plain single column on phones. A developer writes `grid grid-cols-4 md:grid-cols-2` and is surprised phones show four columns. What's the correct class string, and why did theirs fail?
options: `grid grid-cols-4 md:grid-cols-2` is correct; the phone bug is a caching issue
`grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4` — the unprefixed utility is the phone baseline, and prefixes must escalate upward, not start from the widest layout
`grid lg:grid-cols-4 md:grid-cols-2 sm:grid-cols-1` — order the prefixes largest-to-smallest so the cascade resolves correctly
`grid max-md:grid-cols-1 grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4` — you must use a max-width prefix to target phones
variants.rationale: The unprefixed utility is the always-on mobile baseline, so putting `grid-cols-4` bare makes four columns the phone default; `md:grid-cols-2` then only narrows it at ≥768px. Mobile-first means you write the smallest layout unprefixed and layer larger breakpoints on top: `grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4`.
optionExplanations: It isn't correct — bare `grid-cols-4` is the phone baseline, so phones genuinely get four columns; nothing about caching is involved.
Correct — bare utility = mobile baseline, then min-width prefixes escalate: 1 → 2 → 4.

Source order of these utilities doesn't drive the cascade — the min-width media queries do; and `sm:grid-cols-1` still leaves phones below 640px without an explicit baseline. It's the wrong mental model.
A `max-md:` prefix works but is unnecessary and inverts the idiom; the clean mobile-first answer keeps the phone layout unprefixed rather than reaching for max-width overrides.
variants.interviewTip: If you catch yourself writing a breakpoint prefix on the *smallest* layout, stop — the smallest layout should always be the bare, unprefixed utility. Prefixes only ever add larger-screen overrides.

variants.question: A filter sidebar should be visible on desktop and completely absent on phones. A developer writes `<aside class="md:hidden">` — and the sidebar vanishes on desktop while phones still show it, the exact opposite of the goal. What's the correct pairing?
options: `sm:hidden` — the sm prefix targets small screens, so it hides the sidebar on phones
`hidden max-sm:block` — hide by default, then restore it below the sm breakpoint
`hidden md:block` — hidden is the always-on mobile baseline, and `md:block` re-reveals the sidebar from 768px upward
`md:visible hidden` — the visible utility overrides hidden once the md breakpoint is reached
variants.rationale: `md:hidden` reads as 'hide on medium screens' but means 'apply `display: none` from 768px up' — which is why it did the opposite. Mobile-first flips the construction: state the phone reality with a bare utility (`hidden`), then override upward (`md:block`). The developer's version described the desktop and prefixed the phone — backwards on both counts.
optionExplanations: `sm:` is also a min-width prefix — `sm:hidden` hides from 640px *up*, leaving phones showing the sidebar and hiding it on desktop, the same inversion with a different number.
This restores the sidebar *on phones* — precisely the opposite of hiding it there; max-width prefixes exist but this one is aimed the wrong way.
Correct — bare `hidden` handles phones, `md:block` layers the desktop reveal on top: baseline plus upward override.
`visible` sets `visibility: visible`, which cannot undo `display: none` — they're different CSS properties, so the sidebar stays gone at every width.
variants.interviewTip: Every breakpoint prefix silently ends with 'and up'. Reading `md:hidden` aloud as 'hidden from md and up' makes the inversion impossible — verbalizing utilities this way during a pairing session inoculates you against the most common responsive bug.

variants.question: A card is styled `block md:flex lg:grid`. On a 1440px desktop viewport, what is its computed `display` value, and why?
options: `grid` — at 1440px both the `md` and `lg` min-width media queries match simultaneously, and the `lg` rule wins because larger-breakpoint rules are emitted later in the generated stylesheet
`flex` — the `md` query matched first as the viewport was evaluated, and the first matching breakpoint sticks
`block` — the three display utilities conflict, so they cancel out and the unprefixed baseline applies
It's nondeterministic — the winner depends on the order the three classes appear in the class attribute
variants.rationale: Min-width media queries aren't exclusive ranges — at 1440px, `(min-width: 768px)` and `(min-width: 1024px)` are both true, and the unprefixed rule always applies. All three declarations are active; the tie is broken by source order in Tailwind's generated CSS, which emits breakpoints smallest to largest. `lg:grid` sits last, so it wins.
optionExplanations: Correct — overlapping min-width queries all match, and deliberate smallest-to-largest emission order makes the widest matching breakpoint win.
Media queries have no 'first match sticks' semantics — every matching rule applies continuously, and the cascade resolves conflicts by specificity and order, not arrival time.
Conflicting declarations never cancel — the cascade always picks a winner; the baseline only wins below 768px where neither prefixed query matches.
Class-attribute order is irrelevant to the cascade — only the order of rules in the stylesheet matters, which is exactly why utility conflicts can't be resolved by rearranging the className string.
variants.interviewTip: Knowing that `md:` and `lg:` rules are *both active* on a wide screen — and that stylesheet emission order breaks the tie — demonstrates you understand the cascade underneath Tailwind, not just the prefix syntax. It also explains why class-attribute order never matters.

sections.heading: Position, z-index, and where they lie to you
paragraphs: `position: relative` keeps an element in flow but makes it an anchor; `absolute` removes it from flow and positions it against the nearest positioned ancestor; `fixed` pins to the viewport; `sticky` toggles between relative and fixed at a scroll threshold.
z-index looks global but isn't: it only applies to positioned elements (or flex/grid children), and it competes only *within its stacking context*.

A new stacking context is created by more properties than people expect: position+z-index, `transform`, `opacity` below 1, `filter`, `will-change`, and others. Once a parent creates one, its children's z-indexes are trapped inside — they compare against each other, never against the outside world.
sections.summary: A big z-index can't save you if a parent's `transform`, `opacity`, or `filter` traps your element in its own little stacking bubble.

variants.question: A dropdown has z-index: 9999 but still renders underneath a sibling section. The dropdown's parent has `transform: translateX(0)` from an animation. What's going on?
options: Dropdowns must be direct children of body to stack correctly
9999 exceeds the maximum z-index and overflows to a negative value
The transform created a stacking context on the parent; the dropdown's 9999 only competes inside it, and the parent's own stack level loses to the sibling
z-index needs !important to beat sibling elements
variants.rationale: transform (even an identity transform) spawns a stacking context. The dropdown's z-index is now purely internal ranking within that parent; externally, the whole subtree stacks as one unit at the parent's level. Fixes: remove the transform, raise the parent's own stack level, or portal the dropdown out of the trapped subtree.
optionExplanations: Portaling to body is a *workaround* that happens to work by escaping the context — but the stated 'must' rule is false and skips the actual cause.
z-index caps around 2.1 billion and clamps rather than overflows — 9999 is nowhere close.
Correct — 'a child cannot escape its parent's stacking context' is the law behind nearly every mysterious z-index bug.
!important affects cascade specificity (which declaration wins), not stacking order between elements — unrelated mechanisms.
variants.interviewTip: The 'why won't my z-index work' question separates CSS-guessers from CSS-understanders. Name the stacking-context trigger (transform/opacity/filter), then offer the portal escape hatch — React's createPortal exists largely for this.

variants.question: A sticky header with `z-50` mysteriously scrolls *behind* a card lower in the page. The card sits inside a section styled `opacity: 0.98` for a subtle fade, and that section has no z-index at all. Why does a z-index-less card win over a `z-50` header, and what's the cleanest fix?
options: Sticky elements can never stack above their following siblings regardless of z-index — this is expected behavior
The card is winning because it has an implicit `position: absolute`; setting the card to `position: static` fixes it
The header needs a higher value like `z-[9999]`; `z-50` is simply too low to beat the card

`opacity` below 1 made the section a new stacking context that paints as an atomic unit; since that context sits later in the source/paint order than the header's context, its whole subtree — card included — stacks above the header. Remove or rework the `opacity` (e.g. use a background with alpha) so no stacking context is created
variants.rationale: `opacity: 0.98` (any value < 1) establishes a stacking context on the section, which then paints as one indivisible unit against the header. Because that context comes later in paint order and the header isn't lifted above it at the *root* level, the entire section — including a z-index-less card — renders on top. Replacing the opacity fade with a semi-transparent background color (rgba/`bg-…/95`) avoids creating the context, so the header's `z-50` behaves as expected.
optionExplanations: Sticky elements stack by the normal rules; there's no special 'always behind following siblings' behavior — the opacity-induced context is the real cause.
The card has no implicit positioning; opacity, not position, created the context, so toggling `position: static` on the card doesn't address it.
Raising the header's value does nothing when the two elements live in sibling stacking contexts — the header's z-index is only compared inside its own context, not against the section's subtree.
Correct — sub-1 opacity is a stacking-context trigger, and the atomic-paint rule makes the whole section outrank the header regardless of the card's own z-index.
variants.interviewTip: `opacity` and `filter` are the sneakiest stacking-context triggers because they look purely cosmetic. When a z-index fails, scan ancestors of the *other* element for opacity/transform/filter — the culprit is often a sibling subtree, not the element you're debugging.

variants.question: A modal rendered inline inside a settings card uses `fixed inset-0 z-[999]`, yet the page's `sticky top-0 z-40` toolbar still paints over it. The card carries Tailwind's `drop-shadow-xl` (a `filter`). What explains the layering, and what's the standard React fix?
options: `fixed` elements always stack below `sticky` ones; changing the modal to `absolute` restores normal ordering

The card's `filter` spawned a stacking context, so the modal's `z-[999]` only ranks it *within* the card's subtree; against the toolbar, the card's own unremarkable stack level is what competes — render the modal through `createPortal` into `document.body` to escape
Arbitrary values like `z-[999]` aren't generated by the build; replacing it with a canonical `z-50` makes the rule exist
The modal's z-index is fine but too low — bumping it to `z-[99999]` will clear the toolbar's `z-40`
variants.rationale: `drop-shadow-*` utilities apply `filter`, and any filter value establishes a stacking context. From that moment the modal's enormous z-index is purely an internal ranking inside the card; the toolbar compares against the card as a whole, not the modal. Portaling the modal to `document.body` moves it out of the trapped subtree entirely — the canonical reason `createPortal` exists. (As a bonus trap, a filtered ancestor also becomes the containing block for `fixed` descendants, so the 'fixed' modal wasn't even viewport-positioned.)
optionExplanations: No such blanket rule exists — `fixed` and `sticky` elements stack by the ordinary stacking-context rules; position type alone doesn't decide who's on top.
Correct — the filter trapped the modal's z-index inside the card's context, and portaling out of the subtree is the standard escape.
Arbitrary values are fully supported — `z-[999]` is a complete literal token in source, so it's generated like any other class; extraction isn't the issue.
No number helps — the modal's z-index is never compared against the toolbar at all; it's consumed entirely inside the card's stacking context.
variants.interviewTip: Tie the utility to the CSS property: `drop-shadow-*` and `blur-*` are `filter`, and `filter` both spawns a stacking context *and* hijacks `position: fixed` descendants. Naming that double effect turns a debugging war story into a demonstration of spec-level understanding.

variants.question: A tooltip's z-index is trapped because its parent has `will-change: transform`. Which of these, applied to the *tooltip itself*, would let it stack above content outside the parent?
options: `z-[2147483647]` — the maximum z-index value always escalates to the root stacking context
`position: fixed` — fixed positioning re-anchors the tooltip to the viewport's root stacking context
`isolation: isolate` — it re-parents the tooltip into a fresh context at the root level

None of them — no property on a descendant can escape an ancestor's stacking context; the fix must alter the ancestor (drop the `will-change`) or move the tooltip out of the subtree, e.g. via a portal
variants.rationale: Stacking-context membership is structural, not numeric: once an ancestor establishes a context, every descendant's z-index is an internal ranking with no visibility to the outside. There is no CSS property a child can set to break out. The only real fixes operate on the structure — remove the trigger from the ancestor, promote the ancestor's own stack level, or relocate the element (portal) so it was never inside.
optionExplanations: The value clamps at the 32-bit maximum and still only ranks the tooltip against its siblings *inside* the parent's context — magnitude cannot cross a context boundary.

Position type doesn't change context membership — and a `will-change: transform` ancestor additionally becomes the containing block for fixed descendants, so the tooltip wouldn't even anchor to the viewport.
`isolation: isolate` creates a new context *on the element it's applied to*, containing that element's own children — it constrains inward and can never promote outward.
Correct — escape is structural, not stylistic; change the ancestor or move the element, because no descendant-level property crosses the boundary.
variants.interviewTip: The one-liner worth memorizing: 'z-index is a local rank, not a global one.' From it you can immediately reject every big-number and clever-property 'fix' and go straight to the two real levers — the ancestor's trigger, or the element's place in the tree.

sections.heading: Reusable styling without losing the plot
paragraphs: Long class strings are fine until they repeat. The Tailwind-idiomatic cure is extracting a *component* (a Button component owns its classes once), not writing traditional CSS — the reuse unit is the component, not a stylesheet class.

For variants (primary/secondary, sm/lg), keep a small map of complete class strings and select by prop — libraries like cva formalize this. This also stays inside the static-extraction rules from earlier: every class name exists verbatim in source.
Conditional styling composes with template logic: a shared base string plus a selected variant string. Resist string-building fragments of class names; always assemble from whole ones.
sections.summary: When class strings repeat, wrap them in a reusable component and pick variants from a map of whole class strings rather than gluing names together.

variants.question: The same 12-utility class string appears on buttons in 9 files, and a designer just changed the border radius. What's the Tailwind-idiomatic fix going forward?
options: Extract a Button component that owns the class string once; variants become props selecting from complete class strings
Write a .btn class in global CSS and use @apply with all 12 utilities
Shorten the string by dropping the least important utilities
Find-and-replace across the 9 files each time the design changes
variants.rationale: In a component framework, the component *is* the reuse mechanism — one source of truth for the markup and its styling, with variants as typed props. The duplication problem was never about CSS; it was about not having extracted the component.
optionExplanations: Correct — reuse via components, variants via complete-class-string maps.
@apply works but the Tailwind team itself discourages leaning on it — it recreates the named-abstraction indirection Tailwind was designed to avoid. Defensible, not idiomatic.
Deleting styles to reduce duplication changes the design instead of solving the reuse problem.
Manual synchronization across files is exactly the maintenance failure the question demonstrates — the 10th file will be missed.
variants.interviewTip: If asked to critique utility-first CSS ('isn't that just inline styles?'), the strong answer covers: constrained design-scale values, responsive/state variants (`hover:`, `md:`) that inline styles can't express, and components as the reuse layer.

variants.question: A `Badge` component needs three color variants (success/warning/danger) and two sizes (sm/lg). A developer proposes building the class at runtime: `` `px-2 rounded bg-${color}-100 text-${color}-800 ${size === 'lg' ? 'text-lg' : 'text-sm'}` ``. What's the strongest objection, and the idiomatic alternative?
options: The objection is performance — string concatenation on every render is too slow; precompute the string in a useMemo

The `bg-${color}-100` / `text-${color}-800` fragments never appear as complete class names in source, so the build won't generate them; instead keep a map of full class strings per variant (e.g. `success: 'bg-green-100 text-green-800'`) and select by prop — often via a helper like cva
There's no real objection; this is the recommended pattern for variant components in Tailwind
The objection is that inline conditionals are hard to read; extract the ternary into a separate `if` statement but keep the interpolated color fragments
variants.rationale: This collides head-on with static extraction: `bg-${color}-100` is never a complete token in source, so `bg-green-100`, `bg-red-100`, etc. are never generated and the badges render unstyled in the build. The idiomatic fix is a variant→full-class-string map (formalized by cva), where every name like `bg-green-100 text-green-800` appears verbatim, satisfying the scanner while giving you typed variants.
optionExplanations: Performance isn't the issue — the strings are trivially cheap; the real defect is that the interpolated color classes are never generated at build time, so a `useMemo` would just memoize broken class names.
Correct — interpolated color fragments defeat static extraction; a map of complete class strings per variant (cva-style) fixes both the generation problem and gives typed variants.
It is not recommended — the interpolated `bg-${color}-100` fragments are exactly the anti-pattern static extraction forbids.
Cleaning up the ternary readability leaves the fatal flaw untouched: the color fragments are still assembled from pieces and still won't be generated.
variants.interviewTip: Variant components are where the static-extraction rule and the reuse pattern intersect: the reason to prefer a class-string map (or cva) over interpolation isn't just tidiness — it's that interpolated fragments literally fail to compile into CSS.

variants.question: To eliminate duplication, a developer converts the design system into global stylesheet classes — `.card`, `.card-header`, `.btn-primary` — each defined with `@apply` lists of ten-plus utilities, then uses those names throughout the JSX. Reviewers push back. What's the strongest Tailwind-idiomatic critique?
options: @apply output compiles to measurably larger CSS than raw utilities, so the bundle will bloat
Classes built with @apply can't express `hover:` or `md:` states, so all interactivity breaks
The @apply definitions hide the utilities from the production scanner, so the classes get purged from the build

It reconstructs the named-abstraction layer Tailwind exists to avoid — styling drifts out of the markup into a parallel vocabulary you must name, document, and excavate later, when the framework's intended reuse unit is the component that owns its class string exactly once
variants.rationale: The critique isn't technical breakage — @apply works — it's architectural regression. A wall of `.card-header`-style classes reintroduces every cost utility-first was designed to remove: inventing names, hunting definitions in another file, and dead-CSS accumulation. In a component framework the deduplication mechanism already exists: extract a `Card` component that owns the utilities once, and the 'shared class' becomes unnecessary.
optionExplanations: Size differences are marginal and not the point — a critique resting on bytes concedes the architecture and haggles over kilobytes.
False — variants work inside @apply definitions (e.g. `@apply hover:bg-blue-600`); the pattern's problem is indirection, not capability.
Also false — @apply-built classes are compiled directly into the stylesheet and aren't subject to being purged away; inventing a fake technical failure weakens the review.
Correct — the Tailwind team's own guidance: reuse belongs in components (or a variant map), because @apply-heavy stylesheets resurrect the naming-and-indirection tax.
variants.interviewTip: When critiquing a pattern in an interview, concede what works before naming what doesn't: '@apply functions correctly — the cost is architectural, it rebuilds the abstraction layer the tool removed.' Precise concessions make the critique land harder than exaggerated technical claims.

variants.question: A `Button` accepts a `className` prop so callers can override styles. Its base is `px-4 py-2 bg-slate-700`; a caller passes `px-8`, and the rendered element ends up with `class="px-4 py-2 bg-slate-700 px-8"`. Sometimes the override applies, sometimes it doesn't. What actually determines the winner, and what's the robust pattern?
options: The last class in the attribute wins, so `px-8` reliably applies — the flakiness must come from React's re-render ordering
The caller must write `!px-8`; an important modifier is the only supported override mechanism in Tailwind

Attribute order is irrelevant — both utilities have equal specificity, so whichever rule happens to sit later in the *generated stylesheet* wins, which is arbitrary from the component's point of view. Merge with a conflict-aware helper like `tailwind-merge`, or expose typed variant props instead of raw class passthrough
Tailwind deduplicates conflicting utilities at build time and keeps the first occurrence, so the base `px-4` always wins
variants.rationale: The browser treats `class` as an unordered set: with equal specificity, the declaration that appears later in the CSS file wins, and the order of `px-4` vs. `px-8` in Tailwind's output is an implementation detail you don't control. That's why the override 'sometimes works' — it's a coin flip frozen at build time. `tailwind-merge` resolves conflicts in JavaScript before render (last conflicting utility survives), and typed variant props avoid emitting conflicts at all.
optionExplanations: The 'last class in the attribute wins' rule doesn't exist — the class list is a set, and blaming React invents a runtime cause for a stylesheet-order phenomenon.

`!px-8` does force the win, but as a systemic pattern it starts an importance arms race and leaves the dead `px-4` in the markup; it treats a design flaw in the component's API as the caller's problem.
Correct — stylesheet order, not attribute order, decides; conflict-aware merging (or a variants API) is the reliable fix.
No such deduplication pass exists — both rules ship in the stylesheet and both apply; the cascade, not the build, picks the survivor.
variants.interviewTip: 'Why does tailwind-merge exist?' is a sharp interview probe. The answer — className order can't resolve utility conflicts because the cascade goes by stylesheet order at equal specificity — proves you understand the CSS underneath the component API.
